positives: In a million ways. Indie art styles so often give me a sense of enjoyment, comfort, wonder, awe etc.. Repetitive gaming mechanics give me a sense of joy, too. Likewise, story-rich games give me a sense of progress and completion. All of these things contribute so that, overall, gaming gives me a generally very satisfying sense of escapism and joy.
problematic_play: The only ways it negatively contributes to my life is through either its cost or addictiveness. First, on cost, I am a collector for the nintendo switch and I regularly seek out physical games at good prices. But, if I know it's a good price, that means its unlikely to come up like that again any time soon, so I'll buy it almost immediately in most cases. However, this can often cluster such that I find lots of good deals in a short space of time and this costs me too much money, but it's my own fault. Notwithstanding, digitisation has made some physical games much more expensive which is outwith my control and I wish physical formats were supported better. Second, on addictiveness, I am autistic and am very susceptible to over-indulging in repetitive behaviours. I find that games that are repetitive give me a really nice feeling but this can get addictive. As such, I can sink huge amounts into 'infinite' games that cannot be 'completed', like Balatro or Flight Simulator. This can not only consume too much time, but also make me feel guilty for not getting through my backlog of other games that I feel excited about.

Playing Dragon Age helped me realize a lot about myself personally, Dorian was the first time I ever felt like I connected on a personal level to a character and the extremely in-depth character creators that let you make different body types unlocked to faces (aka, a feminine face on a shorter/muscular body) helped me realize I was trans. In short, it can't be overstated how much playing games, silly as it might sound to some, has enriched my life.
problematic_play: My wallet does not feel as enriched as I do over games. Also, when a game series I love and have spent years loving ends up disappointing me, I can literally effect my mental health in a way I wish a video game wouldn't. I mentioned Dragon Age above—when Dragon Age: The Veilguard came out, I preordered the deluxe edition due to having waited nearly a decade for it and feeling like it was a treat. I was so ready to get absorbed in the feel of DA and instead was given something that felt like a whole other IP with Dragon Age embellishments. Another game that did something similar was Genshin Impact. The game started to develop in a way that was disappointing and fostered a fanbase so toxic that I haven't joined a fan community since.

positives:
When enjoyed responsibly (after I have completed all my daily tasks, done a good job at work, and have spent time with my family), gaming is a nice, harmelss reward for my own enjoyment. I don't have to share it with others, but can if I wish. It is one of the few things that is truly "mine", because I give and share everything else with my family. I enjoy sharing things with my family, but y'know. It's nice to have some me-time.

I have autism spectrum disorder and ADHD, and socialization is very difficult for me, even with my husband and son. Gaming gives us something to connect together with. I can live stream my game (privately via an unlisted youtube link, not for other viewers) to my son and husband, while being in a private voice call together. This allows us to have our own space, while still enjoying time together. 

Of course, we still go on vacation, socialize ~95% of the time face to face, etc. Gaming is more of a supplement, and not a replacement for family time. I think that gaming can be a problem, like any hobby. You can spend too much money, too much time, care about it more than the people in your life, become addicted, etc. But, it can also be a reprieve from the difficulties of the world, as long as you are using it in tandem with other life management skills, and not as a replacement for friends, a life, real hobbies, etc. 

 This is all just my personal experience with gaming, and I'm not trying to cast a wide net over the general public, here. Thanks for listening!

positives: Games are an art form I enjoy engaging in, and I find gaming fun, interesting, expressive, intellectually stimulating, and often emotionally cathartic or stimulating (especially if the game has a good story). Games allow me to explore situations, places, and experiences I wouldn't have in real-life, and often, either the option to express myself in new ways (with avatar characters or other customizable elements), or the option to be someone else for a while. They often allow me to enter a satisfying and cathartic flow state that gives me a break from other things going on in my head or in my life, and that is engaging in it's own right. It can be quite mediative, and weirdly, I have found that engaging with interesting actions, places, and stories in games helps me be mindful not just in the game but in real-life, as well - it helps me appreciate such things in the real world, too. Games also inspire me to create my own art and write my own stories, both literally and figuratively. Overall, I typically consider gaming a worthwhile use of time (as long as I like/connect with the game I'm playing), and I find my mental health is generally better when I reserve some time for gaming.
problematic_play: I have ADHD and OCD, and sometimes I can get hyperfixated on a game. This doesn't usually cause problems (due to my loose work schedule), and is often an enjoyable experience, but it can occasionally lead to more time spent gaming than intended. Though typically I game when I might otherwise be doing other down-time activities like watching TV/YouTube or reading, not when I would otherwise be working, so it's not usually too disruptive to work, but it can occasionally be disruptive to sleep. Probably the biggest challenge gaming contributes to my life is to my wallet. Because I'm so interested in the experiences offered by games (not necessarily in mastering or completing them all), I have a hard time resisting the urge to buy lots of different games.
